questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'. I cannot understand that you are trying to say.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.

I cannot understand that you are trying to say.
questions.solution:
The correct answer 'what you'.

Key Points

  • A noun clause functions as a noun in a sentence.
  • It follows a linking or copular verb to describe or modify the subject of a sentence.
  • Unlike Noun phrases, noun clauses contain both a subject and a verb.
    • For example: Do you know what time it is?
  • In the example given above the bolded noun clauses are dependent clauses.
  • In the given sentence 'that you are trying to say' is a noun clause.
  • In this sentence, the most appropriate pronoun will be 'what' instead of 'that' because 'understand' does not take a 'that-clause.'
  • We can use 'what' as a pronoun to mean 'the thing that'.
  • Hence, option 2 is the correct answer.

 

The correct sentence: I cannot understand what you are trying to say.

Additional Information

  • A noun clause can be used as the subject, direct object, indirect object, object of a preposition, subject complement, or appositive.
    • Example:
      • Subject: What I had forgotten was that I had a test today.
      • Direct Object: You must choose which flavor of ice cream you want. 

Hinglish

  • Noun clause वाक्य में संज्ञा के रूप में कार्य करता है।
  • यह एक वाक्य के विषय का वर्णन करने या संशोधित करने के लिए एक linking or copular verb का अनुसरण करता है।
  • Noun phrases के विपरीत, noun clauses में एक subject और एक verb दोनों होते हैं।
    • उदाहरण: Do you know what time it is?
  • ऊपर दिए गए उदाहरण में bold हिस्सा noun clause dependent clause हैं।
  • दिए गए वाक्य में 'that you are trying to say' एक noun clause है।
  • इस वाक्य में सबसे उपयुक्त pronoun 'what' होगा क्योंकि 'understanding' शब्द 'that-clause' नहीं लेता है।
  • हम 'what' का उपयोग pronoun के रूप में 'the thing that' कहने के लिए कर सकते हैं।
  • अतः विकल्प 2 सही उत्तर है।
  • एक noun clause का उपयोग subject, direct object, indirect object, object of a preposition, subject complement, or appositive के रूप में किया जा सकता है।
    • उदाहरण:  
      • Subject: What I had forgotten was that I had a test today.
      • Direct Object: You must choose which flavor of ice cream you want. 
 

सही वाक्य: I cannot understand what you are trying to say.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No improvement’. For the last two years Shweta has being diligently working with Rohingya refugees to create colourful table mats using their local weaving techniques.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No improvement’.

For the last two years Shweta has being diligently working with Rohingya refugees to create colourful table mats using their local weaving techniques.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'has been'.

Key Points

  • The usage of 'being' is wrong in the given sentence.
  • The given sentence is in the present perfect continuous tense and 'has been' is used in the present perfect continuous tense.
    • E.g. Girish has been working in this company for two years.
  • According to the rule and example that are given above, 'has been' will be used in the underlined part of the sentence.
    ​

Correct Sentence: For the last two years Shweta has been diligently working with Rohingya refugees to create colourful table mats using their local weaving techniques.

Additional Information

  • The present perfect continuous tense shows that something started in the past and is continuing at the present time.
  • The present perfect continuous is formed using the construction "has/have been + v1 + ing + for/ since + time".
    • E.g. we have been living in this house since 2007.
  • Usage of 'since' and 'for':
    • Since is used for a point of time. 
      • Since Monday, since, 2002, since, last year.
    • For is used for a period of time.
      • For the last two years, for the last 3 weeks

questions.question: Select the appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed word in the following sentence to make it grammatically correct. The grapes taste ( sweetest ). .
questions.questionHtml:
Select the appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed word in the following sentence to make it grammatically correct.

The grapes taste (sweetest)..
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'sweet'.
 
Key Points 
  • The verb "taste" in this sentence is a linking verb. Linking verbs connect the subject to a word or phrase that describes or identifies the subject.
  • When a linking verb is used, it should be followed by an adjective that describes the subject, not an adverb. The adjective tells us about the state or quality of the subject (the grapes).
  • "Sweet" is an adjective in its positive degree.
  • "Sweetest" is the superlative degree of the adjective, used when comparing three or more things. The sentence is not making a comparison, nor is it implying that these grapes are the sweetest among all grapes. It's simply describing their taste.
Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.
 
Complete Sentence: "The grapes taste sweet."
 
Additional Information 
  • Option 1: "more sweeter" – This is grammatically incorrect. "Sweeter" is already the comparative form; adding "more" makes it a double comparative.
  • Option 2: "sweeter" – This is the comparative degree, used when comparing two things (e.g., "These grapes taste sweeter than those"). The original sentence doesn't imply a comparison.
  • Option 4: "most sweeter" – This is also grammatically incorrect, being a double comparative with the superlative form.

questions.question: In the following sentence the underlined part contains an error. Alternatives to the underlined part are given as options. Select the correct alternative. The new almirah is big than this one.
questions.questionHtml:
In the following sentence the underlined part contains an error. Alternatives to the underlined part are given as options. Select the correct alternative.
The new almirah is big than this one.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 1.
 
Key Points
  • The primary issue in the sentence is the incorrect comparative form of the adjective "big."
  • Comparative adjectives are used to compare differences between the two objects they modify (larger, smaller, faster, higher).
  • The correct comparative form of "big" is "bigger."
  • Thus, the sentence should be corrected to "bigger than this one."
Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.
 
Correct Sentence: "The new almirah is bigger than this one."
 
Additional Information
  • Option 2: "more big" is incorrect because "big" is a one-syllable adjective, and for one-syllable adjectives, we add "-er" to make the comparative form.
  • Option 3: "biggest" is incorrect because "biggest" is the superlative form, used to compare more than two items or people.
  • Option 4: "more bigger" is incorrect because it is a double comparative, which is grammatically incorrect.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment. If no substitution is required select 'No substitution' If I would have a degree from the university, I would get a good job.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment. If no substitution is required select 'No substitution'

If I would have a degree from the university, I would get a good job.

options.text: If I am having the degree
options.html: If I am having the degree

options.text: When I will have a degree
options.html: When I will have a degree

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: If I had a degree.

Key Points

  • The phrase "If I had a degree" is an example of a conditional statement in the past tense. It expresses a hypothetical situation or a condition that is contrary to reality. In this case, the speaker is saying that if they had a degree, they believe that they would have a better chance of getting a good job. However, since the speaker does not currently have a degree, it implies that they do not currently have a good job or may have limited job opportunities.
  • This type of conditional statement is known as a second conditional or Type 2 conditional, which is used to talk about hypothetical or unlikely situations in the present or future.
  • The incident that happens first or was supposed to happen first takes a past tense (V2 form of verb) in the ‘If’ clause when ‘would/could/should + V1’ is present in the main clause (result).
    • For example: If I had a bike, I would reach on time.
  • Similarly, in this context, 'had' (V2) should be in the 'If' clause because 'would + V1' (would get) is in the main clause.
  • Hence, 'If I had a degree' is the correct set of words that must substitute the underlined segment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: If I had a degree from the university, I would get a good job.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can rectify the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to rectify it, select ‘no rectification needed’. The conductor said that it was the worse quake he ever knew.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can rectify the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to rectify it, select ‘no rectification needed’.

The conductor said that it was the worse quake he ever knew.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: worst.

Key Points

  • In the given sentence, the word "worse" is incorrect when comparing it to past experiences of the conductor.
  • Instead, the superlative form "worst" should be used to indicate that this earthquake was the most severe one the conductor had ever experienced.
  • Superlative adjectives are used to describe an object which is at the upper or lower limit of a quality (e.g., the tallest, the smallest, the fastest, the highest).
  • The sentence should read: "The conductor said that it was the worst quake he ever knew."

Hence, the correct answer is option 4.

Correct sentence: The conductor said that it was the worst quake he ever knew.

Additional Information

  • When comparing two objects, use the comparative form of the adjective (e.g., better, worse).
  • When comparing more than two objects, use the superlative form of the adjective (e.g., best, worst).
  • Examples:
    • This is the best book I have ever read.
    • Out of the three runners, she is the fastest.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'. Rohit had hardly stepped into the office than he was summon by his boss.

questions.solution:

Key Points

  • In the given sentence, the conjunction 'than' is incorrect here.
  • Also, the verb was will not work with summon.

  • We need to use the conjunction when which implies 'at that time'.
  • It also completes the meaning of the first clause of the sentence by indicating the time when Rohit's boss summoned him.
  • The verb 'was' should be used with the past participle form summoned in the given sentence.

The correct sentence is: Rohit had hardly stepped into the office when he was summoned by his boss.

Hence, the correct answer is option 2.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'. The miscreants were shifted to another building that same evening and was keeping in custody by the police.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1) i.e., 'were kept'.

Key Points

  • The underlined part of the given sentence is incorrect as was keeping is the past continuous tense form of the verb keep. 
  • The given sentence is in simple past tense form and so the past continuous tense form cannot be used. 
  • The simple past tense form of keep is kept. 
  • We need to use the linking verb were as the sentence deals with the third person plural (they for the miscreants → (they) were kept).
  • So, option 1 is the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

So the correct sentence is- The miscreants were shifted to another building that same evening and were kept in custody by the police.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. France is a largest country.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

France is a largest country.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'large'.
 
Key Points
  • The error in the sentence is the incorrect usage of the article "a" with a superlative adjective.
  • "A" should be followed by an adjective, not a superlative form.
  • The word "largest" is a superlative and should usually be preceded by "the," not "a."
  • The correct form should be "France is a large country," using the simple adjective "large" instead of the superlative.
Therefore, the correct answer is ‘Option 4’.
 
Correct Sentence: France is a large country.
 
Additional Information
  • smaller: This option is incorrect because it changes the meaning of the sentence entirely. The sentence intends to describe France as a large country, not a smaller one
  • larger: This option is not suitable because it is a comparative adjective. The sentence does not compare France to another country.
  • smallest: This option is incorrect because it is a superlative adjective and does not fit the context of the sentence. It would describe France as the smallest, which is incorrect based on the intended meaning.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No correction required’. Everyone sincerely and positively were ready to find the solution for the serious issue of sewage system.

Everyone sincerely and positively were ready to find the solution for the serious issue of sewage system.
questions.solution: The subject of the sentence is "Everyone," which is a singular pronoun. In English grammar, singular subjects require singular verbs. Adverbs (such as "sincerely" and "positively" in this case) typically come after the verb "to be." Placing them after the verb is a common and accepted structure. "Everyone was sincerely and positively" maintains subject-verb agreement and follows the standard order for adverb placement after the verb.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. I have lost my school diary; I can’t find it nowhere .
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

I have lost my school diary; I can’t find it nowhere.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'anywhere'.

Key Points

  • The given sentence is grammatically incorrect.
  • Here, 'anywhere' should be used instead of 'nowhere'.
  • It means 'in, at or to any place.' (कहीं भी, कहीं पर भी)
    • Example: I can’t find my keys anywhere.
  • The first clause of the given sentence clearly states that the school diary is lost. Hence, it couldn't be found at any place.
  • A negative word i.e. 'not' has already been used in the sentence. Thus, we cannot use another negative word 'nowhere'.
  • Hence, 'anywhere' should be used.
     

Correct Sentence: I have lost my school diary; I can't find it anywhere.

Additional Information

  • Let's look at the meaning of other words:
    • Wherever: in or to any place. [जहाँ कहीं (किसी भी स्‍थान में या पर)]
    • Everywhere: in or to every place. (सब जगह, सर्वत्र)
    • Somewhere: at, in, or to a place that you do not know or do not mention by name. [स्थान पर जो आपको नहीं मालूम या जिसका नाम आप नहीं बताते; कहीं]

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence. Had you been to Dubai, I would also go with you.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.

Had you been to Dubai, I would also go with you.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: I would have gone.

The marked option correctly uses the past perfect tense "would have gone," which matches the conditional "Had you been" in the sentence.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’. Had you not interfering in my affairs, I would have been in the US now.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.

Had you not interfering in my affairs, I would have been in the US now.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Had you not interfered'

Key Points

  • The given sentence is a third conditional sentence in which the structure is- Had + subject + third form of the verb, Subject + would + have + V3
  • Hence, we need to use the third form of the verb 'interfere' i.e. 'interfered'
  • Hence, the correct sentence is Had you not interfered in my affairs, I would have been in the US now.

Additional Information

  • Mostly the students get confused with 'had had' structure also when the sentence has single 'had'.
  • Had had- means the former had is an auxiliary verb and the latter had is a main verb i.e. third form of the verb 'have'
    • She felt marvelous after she had had a good night’s sleep.
  • 'had'- whenever the subordinate clause has single 'had' then we quickly understand that the sentence belongs to second conditional.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. If I was the queen , I would give a handsome sum towards education.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.
If I was the queen, I would give a handsome sum towards education.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: were the queen. 

Explanation: In hypothetical or contrary-to-fact statements, the subjunctive mood is used. "Were" is the correct form to indicate a hypothetical situation.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. Arushya purchased the most good of all the suits kept in the shop.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Arushya purchased the most good of all the suits kept in the shop.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 2.
 
Key Points
  • The primary issue in the sentence is the incorrect usage of "most good."
  • The correct superlative form of "good" is "best."
  • The correct phrase should be "the best" to represent the superlative degree correctly.
  • Thus, the most appropriate substitution is the best.
Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.
 
Correct Sentence: "Arushya purchased the best of all the suits kept in the shop."
 
Additional Information
  • Option 1: "the goods" – This option is incorrect because "goods" refers to items or products, not the superlative degree of "good".
  • Option 3: "the more good" – This option is grammatically incorrect because "more good" is not a proper comparative or superlative form.
  • Option 4: "the good" – This option lacks the superlative degree needed to convey that Arushya purchased the best suit.

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement. So much as you behave like this, the decision of the management against you cannot be revoked.
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement.

So much as you behave like this, the decision of the management against you cannot be revoked.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "​as long as".

  • In the given underlined segment, the use of "So much as" is incorrect as "so...as" can only be used with negative like 'not'.
  • We use not + so + adjective/adverb + as to make comparisons, meaning not to the same degree.
  • But we use as + adjective/adverb + as to make comparisons when the things we are comparing are equal in some way.
  • We use "as long as" to refer to the intended duration of a plan or idea, most commonly referring to the future. We always use the present simple to refer to the future after "as long as".
  • Hence, the correct answer is option 4.
     

Correct Sentence: As long as you behave like this, the decision of the management against you cannot be revoked.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No Improvement. She give me everything I asked for.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No Improvement.

She give me everything I asked for.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2), i.e., Gave me everything.

 ​Explanation:

  •  The sentence uses the incorrect simple present tense verb 'Give'.
  •  The second verb of the sentence is the simple past tense 'asked'.
  •  Given the context, the first verb here should also be in its simple past tense form, 'Gave'.
  •  Extra Point:
  •  Note that present perfect 'has given' and past perfect 'had given' are also grammatically correct forms in this case.


Thus, the rectified sentence is: She gave me everything I asked for.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No Improvement. You need have brought your umbrella as it is a cloudy day.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No Improvement.

You need have brought your umbrella as it is a cloudy day.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Should have'

Key Points

  • The sentence is suggesting that an umbrella should have been brought.
  • The modal used for expressing expectation/suggestion is 'should'.
  • The modal 'need' expresses the obligation or necessity.

So the correct sentence: You should have brought your umbrella as it is a cloudy day.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. Even if you’ve never heard his name, you’ve probably met someone with his words tattooed in their skin or heard them sung at a music concert.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Even if you’ve never heard his name, you’ve probably met someone with his words tattooed in their skin or heard them sung at a music concert.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 4.
 
Key Points
  • The primary issue in the sentence is the incorrect preposition "in" used with the verb "tattooed."
  • The correct preposition to use with "tattooed" is "on," as tattoos are typically placed on the surface of the skin.
  • The correct phrase should be "tattooed on their skin" to convey the intended meaning correctly.
  • Thus, the most appropriate substitution is tattooed on their skin.
Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.
 
Correct Sentence: "Even if you’ve never heard his name, you’ve probably met someone with his words tattooed on their skin or heard them sung at a music concert."
 
Additional Information
  • Option 1: "tattooed through their skin" – This option is incorrect as "through their skin" implies piercing or going completely through, which is not the intended meaning.
  • Option 2: "tattooed until their skin" – This option is grammatically incorrect and does not make sense in the given context.
  • Option 3: "tattooed overdoing their skin" – This option is incorrect because "overdoing their skin" is not a valid or meaningful phrase.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’. The film was made in Botswana, whose wildlife parks is larger to those in Kenya.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.

The film was made in Botswana, whose wildlife parks is larger to those in Kenya.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: are larger than.

The marked option is correct because "parks" is plural, so it should be "are" instead of "is," and "larger" is the correct comparative form to use with "than."

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined segment in the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement' How much does it cost to travels from the airport to Noida?
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined segment in the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'

How much does it cost to travels from the airport to Noida?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'travel'.

Key Points

  • In the given sentence we can see the use of the preposition 'to'.
  • Whenever a verb follows the preposition 'to', it is always used in its base form.
    • Let's understand with the help of some examples:
      • She's not strong enough to go hiking up mountains.
      • This tool is used to make holes in leather.
      • This meat is difficult to chew.
      • Can you tell me how to get there?
  • Therefore the word 'travels' must be replaced with 'travel' to make the sentence grammatically correct.

Correct sentence: How much does it cost to travel from the airport to Noida?

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence. The company do not broke the law at any time.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.

The company do not broke the law at any time.
questions.solution: The correct answer is: does not break. The marked option is correct grammatically because "does" is the appropriate auxiliary verb for the present tense with a singular subject "company," and "break" is the correct base form of the verb.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate form of comparative degree that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. Bilingual children are so intelligent than those who speak just one language.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate form of comparative degree that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Bilingual children are so intelligent than those who speak just one language.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '3' i.e. more intelligent than .

Key Points

  • The given sentence uses a comparative degree to compare the intelligence of bilingual children to those who speak just one language.
  • The correct comparative form of "intelligent" is "more intelligent."
  • The word "than" is used after the comparative form to show the comparison.

Correct sentence: Bilingual children are more intelligent than those who speak just one language.

Additional Information

  • Comparative Degree:
    • Usage: Used to compare differences between the two objects they modify (larger, smaller, faster, higher). They are used in sentences where two nouns are compared, in this pattern: Noun (subject) + verb + comparative adjective + than + noun (object).
    • Examples:
      • She is taller than her brother.
      • This car is faster than that one.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’. Children need much of guidance in how to use the internet wisely and efficiently.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.

Children need much of guidance in how to use the internet wisely and efficiently.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'a lot'.

Key Points

  • The correct option to replace 'much' in this sentence is 'a lot'.
  • 'a lot of' and 'much' can both be used to express large quantities. However, their usage depends on the context and the type of noun they modify.
  • 'A lot of' can be used with both countable and uncountable nouns in affirmative sentences.
  • In this sentence, the word 'guidance' is an uncountable noun, and it's in an affirmative sentence.
  • Hence, the use of 'a lot' is most appropriate in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Children need a lot of guidance in how to use the internet wisely and efficiently.

Additional Information

  • 'much' is typically used with uncountable nouns in negative sentences or questions. However, the use of the preposition 'of' after 'much' is grammatically incorrect in this context.
  • Similarly, the use of 'most' would be incorrect as the use of the preposition 'of' after 'most' is grammatically incorrect in this context.
  • 'many' is used with countable nouns, not uncountable nouns like 'guidance'.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. Rashmi works at the hospital, don’t she ?
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Rashmi works at the hospital, don’t she?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'doesn't she?.

Key Points

  • In the second part of the given sentence, the singular form of the verb 'don’t' is incorrect.
  • In the given sentence, the correct tag question should use 'doesn’t she?' as Rashmi is a singular subject.
  • Tag questions are formed using the auxiliary verb from the statement, and since Rashmi works (present tense), the correct auxiliary is 'does'.
  • Hence, the correct form of the verb 'doesn’t' should be used in place of the incorrect form 'don’t'.
     

Therefore, the correct answer is option 3.

Correct sentence: Rashmi works at the hospital, doesn’t she?.

Additional Information

  • If the subject in the statement is singular and the verb is in the present tense, the correct auxiliary verb in the tag question should be 'does' followed by 'not' if the statement is positive.
  • If the subject in the statement is plural and the verb is in the present tense, the correct auxiliary verb in the tag question should be 'do' followed by 'not' if the statement is positive.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’. He was so curious that he rose many questions in the meeting.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.

He was so curious that he rose many questions in the meeting.
questions.solution: 'Raised' is the right verb form, not 'rose' or 'aroused'. 'Many questions' is accurate because 'much' is used for uncountable nouns and 'many' is used for countable nouns. Thus, option 2 is the right choice. The correct sentence should be "He was so curious that he raised many questions in the meeting."

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. I don't know why he is such secretly.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

I don't know why he is such secretly.
questions.solution: In Subject-verb agreement, In the given sentence, we need a singular verb "is" with a singular pronoun "he" and an adverb "so" that modifies the adjective "secretive".

questions.question: Direction: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. In order to enhancing their reputation , companies are investing a lot of money in social initiatives.
questions.questionHtml:
Direction: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

In order to enhancing their reputation, companies are investing a lot of money in social initiatives.
questions.solution: The error in the sentence is the incorrect use of the verb form after the preposition "to." Here, "enhance" is the base form of the verb used after the preposition "to." Structure: to + base form of the verb. Example: I want to leave the house. The correct form of the verb in this case is the base form, not the gerund form. Correct sentence: In order to enhance their reputation, companies are investing a lot of money in social initiatives.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement. A fire broke out in a slum cluster in the capital yesterday for short circuit at the overhanging wires.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement.

A fire broke out in a slum cluster in the capital yesterday for short circuit at the overhanging wires.

options.text: for short circuit in the the overhanging wires.
options.html: for short circuit in the the overhanging wires.

options.text: due to short circuit in the overhanging wires.
options.html: due to short circuit in the overhanging wires.

options.text: due to short circuiting on the overhanging wires.
options.html: due to short circuiting on the overhanging wires.

questions.solution:
The sentence mentions an incident and also the reason behind that incident.

From the given options, the correct way of illustrating a reason is by using due to in that sentence. This makes option 1 wrong.

Now, in option 3, short-circuiting is mentioned which is wrong because short-circuit itself is a Process and the reason for the fire breaking out. We don't have to use continuous ('ing') form there. Also, short-circuiting on the wires is wrong, it happened in (i.e. inside) the wires. So, option 3 is wrong. 

Hence, option 2 is the correct answer.

questions.question: Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. Identify which set of words must replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct. He is good at playing the guitar than his brother.
questions.questionHtml:
Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. Identify which set of words must replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct.

He is good at playing the guitar than his brother.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: is better.

Key Points

  • The given sentence compares the abilities of two people: "He" and "his brother".
  • In comparative sentences, the correct form to use is "better" instead of "good".
  • The word "than" indicates a comparison, so the adjective should be in its comparative form.
  • Therefore, "good" should be changed to "better" to correctly express the comparison.

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Correct sentence: He is better at playing the guitar than his brother.

questions.question: Select the correct option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. This secret will remain between you and I.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the correct option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

This secret will remain between you and I.
questions.solution: The correct answer: Between you and me. Explanation: The correct pronoun to use after a preposition like "between" is "me," not "I." Hence, "between you and me" is grammatically correct.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. The performance of the musicians was rather worst than expected by the audience.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

The performance of the musicians was rather worst than expected by the audience.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Option 3' i.e. worse than expected is the correct usage.

Key Points

  • The original sentence uses "rather worst than expected," which is grammatically incorrect.
  • The comparative form "worse" should be used instead of the superlative form "worst" when making comparisons between two states.
  • "Worse than expected" correctly conveys that the performance did not meet the audience's expectations.
  • The correction maintains the meaning of the original sentence while correcting its grammatical structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is- Correct answer

Additional Information

  • "Worst than expectation" is incorrect because "worst" is a superlative form and the phrase is awkwardly constructed.
  • "Worse was expected" changes the sentence structure unnecessarily and does not fit grammatically into the original sentence.
  • "Bad as expected" does not convey the comparative degree that is needed to show that the performance was below expectations.
  • The correct usage of comparative and superlative forms is crucial for maintaining the grammatical integrity of a sentence.
